utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. I think this morning we prefer to start with what counsel has suggested, because I have before me, and all my brother judges have, a motion for decision on presentation of evidence. I believe the prosecution also has it. It calls for an interpretation of Rule 85 affecting cross-examination and the rights of the defence with respect to cross-examination. I fear that if we ignore this and carry on without disposing of it, it might create more difficulties, especially since a very serious allegation has been made in the motion by counsel that we are behaving differently from Trial Chamber 1 and that this is causing prejudice to the defence. Actually I did not want to bother with that aspect, because there has been a manifest error in knowing in which Trial Chamber we are sitting. Trial Chamber 1 has not come to any decision on it. We are part of Trial Chamber 2. I think it is better to correct that first time. I do not know whether the prosecution is prepared to respond to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did receive it I believe yesterday and have prepared a response, which is being typed now. I can briefly summarise our response if your Honours wish, or we would be able to file a response today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: As I have stated, it is better we put it out of the way before another cross-examination arises, because it will complicate matters if we are found to be wrong in what we are doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In that case, your Honour, let me briefly -- I do not even have a copy of the draft -- our draft response or the motion of the accused at the present time, but I can briefly tell you that our position is that there is no conflict between any of the Trial Chambers, that there is nothing in the rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is all right. When you are ready, we will hear your response and you can file your written response. You can make your response later. The response will be filed when it is typed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you like to hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We would like to hear it right now, yes. Reply by the Prosecution

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Briefly our response is that there is no conflict between the Trial Chambers, that there is nothing in the rules which requires that there be re-cross-examination. Indeed, the rules seem to contemplate there will not be re-cross-examination, but all in all it is a matter for the discretion of the Trial Chamber, depending on the circumstances. It may have been that because of the proceedings in the Tadic trial and because of the manner in which cross-examination was conducted that the Trial Chamber thought it would not create problems to allow limited re-cross, and, fact, this Chamber may in certain circumstances, in particular where unexpectedly some new issue is raised during re-direct, the Trial Chamber might choose to do such a thing, but that in general it should be a very rare and exceptional situation, that thus far in this Chamber there has been no need for such re-cross. The issues brought up in re-direct -- often there has not been any re-direct. In the few occasions where there was, it was very limited with a limited purpose. This Chamber has an obligation to ensure that proceedings are conducted in a fair and expeditious manner. This Chamber has been very, very free in giving defence counsel rein in cross-examination, and under these circumstances the Trial Chamber has appropriately used its discretion to not allow it. Obviously there may be rare situations in the future where the Chamber may decide to allow it. I would just also point out that, for instance, the defendant Landzo, who makes this argument, previously had filed a Bill of Exceptions with respect to one of the first -- I believe one of the expert witnesses for the model and the photographs, and the defence counsel had filed a Bill of Exceptions, stating forth numerous questions that the defence of Esad Landzo would have asked if they had been allowed re-cross. I think looking at those questions makes it very clear that those questions were entirely inappropriate to be raised in re-cross-examination, that to the extent the questions were relevant at all, they should have been raised in cross-examination, and there was absolutely nothing in the re-direct which would have made such questions even proper. So, in sum, our position is there is no conflict among the Trial Chambers. It is up to the discretion of the Trial Chamber. In these circumstances, the Trial Chamber has appropriately used its discretion to not permit it, so that we may have a fair and expeditious trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we hear you now, Ms McMurrey? Reply by Ms McMurrey

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. If you will just allow me to respond, of course I think my motion is fairly clear. Ms McHenry and the prosecution alleges that there is no conflict between the two Trial Chambers, and I did not spend days looking through the Tadic record. I just picked out two, the first two that came up quickly, and I believe that it is evident from the Tadic record that there is a conflict. Direct examination, cross, re-direct, re-cross were allowed many times in that case, and in this case we have tried to have re-cross, as was allowed in Tadic, and I have been denied re-cross, as have the other defence attorneys. I did make a Bill of Exceptions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think you have still not understood your initial error, that the Tadic Trial Chamber is not different from this one. You still have not understood that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Would you clear that up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not Trial Chamber 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then the judges' decisions within each trial -- I do not know what to call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I just want to correct that error. I do not want to correct the other errors. There are so many of them. I just want to correct it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I hope the court corrects me if I use the wrong nomenclature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not a training school. Go about your argument.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The decisions in the first trial are clearly different from the decisions in the second trial on the presentation of evidence. Under Rule 85B the rule says exactly: "Examination-in-chief is allowed. Cross-examination and re-examination shall be allowed in each case." Now my interpretation of that is that "in each case" means the defence case and the prosecution case, and that is where I think it does allow for re-cross or "rejoinder", as it calls it, as the rule allows, once they are -- if the prosecution decides to re-direct, then we have a right to re-cross, and vice versa. When we are presenting our evidence in the defence case, if we decide to re-direct, then the prosecution has a right to re-cross. I believe that is explained, of course subject to interpretation, and each one of the panels of judges of course has the discretion to decide their own rules, but since there is a discrepancy now, and when the presentation of evidence is allowed re-cross in one trial and it does not allow re-cross in the other, then I believe it does create a prejudice for the people trying the case in the next Trial Chamber or group of judges. I do not know what to call it. As such, there just needs to be a decision made, so that there is consistency between each trial as we go along. I am not saying that the other court was right, and I am not saying that this court is right, but I noticed ahead of time that that was the rule of the first trial, and that is why I assumed it was going to be the rule of the second trial. If the court makes a decision there is going to be no rejoinder, I will simply make a Bill of Exception for each witness to preserve error for the Appeals Court, but I agree with Ms McHenry that re-cross-examination is limited to the scope of re-direct, and it narrows everything down until, hopefully, everybody has answered all their questions. Now, because we were denied re-cross on certain witnesses, we have a right to recall that witness in our defence -- when we present our defence case in chief. I think, so that we do not have to bring witnesses back from Bosnia or the United States or wherever they might be, it would be more expeditious and economical just to let us finish with that witness while he is here. Let us just go all the way with any questions we might have, and then we have no reason to recall that witness later on. I am asking the court just for a decision. Whatever your decision, the defence will abide by it, but there is a difference between the procedures in the two trials. I would just like clarification for myself as to which way we are going to proceed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you refer to other judicial jurisdictions, like the United States, Canada, Scotland. You are sure this practice exists there as a general rule?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know from the United States -- I have tried at least 50 criminal trials -- I know we are allowed re-cross and re-direct until we finish with the witness. I was also advised that Australia has the same rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe there are a lot of other common law countries that have the same proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I come from a common law country.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You could ask Mr O'Sullivan -- he comes from Canada -- and I am speaking from my experience in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: And Scotland too?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That is what I was told by Mr Greaves, who comes from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If you ask Ms McHenry, who comes from the United States, she will agree that is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am not sure I can agree. I have tried many trials, but I have been here so long I cannot remember. My memory is it is up to the discretion of the Trial Chamber and sometimes Trial Chambers determine it is not appropriate. The other thing I would say is I do not believe in Tadic they had a specific rule in every case, nor do I believe this Chamber has adopted a special rule. For instance, I will point out that yesterday defence counsel was allowed re-cross-examination. The issue is not: is there going to be one rule? The issue is: what are the circumstances as determined by the Trial Chamber as to what is appropriate, and I do not believe that there is anything else that can and should be done in this Trial Chamber in limiting it in the cases where it has -- has acted entirely appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing further. I was very happy to be able to cross-examine yesterday on the medical document that was brought up, and I believe that that is the way the procedure should be when an issue is raised, that we should have the ability to question that witness further on a document. I am only asking for what the court did allow yesterday as things proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other contribution on this, because it is one of general importance?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just quickly, I think we have a seam between the traditions in various common law countries. As far as I know it is the universal practice in the United States and every court I have ever practised in to allow re-cross and re-direct, narrowed down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: As a general rule or exceptionally?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is always allowed in every trial I have ever had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Even if there is no need for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a rule --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Even re-examination is based on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You will have to bring yourself within that re-examination for other cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How is it as a general rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As a general rule if there is a relevant question that is directly related to the re-direct examination, it is universally allowed in any court I have practised in in the United States. When Mr Greaves told me earlier this week that it was not the practice in England and Wales I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Definitely not. I happened to be called in England in 1961. Quite frankly their practice is never so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I agree when Mr Greaves told me there was a different rule in England and Wales, I did not know that. I have checked with Professor O'Sullivan this morning, and he tells me that in Canada typically the prosecutor does not object to a re-cross-examination, for what that is worth. It is always a narrow procedure, your Honour. It is not a wide open re-cross-examination to ask anything you want to, and the court, of course, maintains control. If it starts getting far afield, the court is authorised to cut it off, if it starts confusing the issues or if it is a needless waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Primarily we are bound by our own rules, the way our rules have been formulated. That is what we thought. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do not know whether you would feel any offering from me would be helpful, but I confirm that the General rule in England and Wales is, as your Honour knows, examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination. There is, however, a residual discretion in the trial judge. For example, if counsel has sat down and he has forgotten a crucial matter, it is perfectly open to him to get up and say: "With your Honour's leave might I just ask one further question?" It would be a very hard prosecutor indeed who would say: "I object to that course being followed." Effectively there is a residual discretion in the court to say: "Please by all means ask those further questions." Of course then prosecuting counsel can re-examine on those matters as well. I am not qualified in Scotland, but I believe the system to be the same here. I believe my learned friend Ms McMurrey misunderstood what I was saying. I think that was more to do with other characteristics of Scottish trial procedures. I believe that in other jurisdictions, such as New Zealand, Australia, they follow the English system, and I suspect in your Honour's own jurisdiction in Nigeria you follow that system as well. From my point of view I prepare my case the English way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am a lawyer from the civil system in Sweden, as you may know. We have no firm rules. The party who brings a witness examines that witness in chief, and then there is a right to examination from the other party, and then it is only a question of relevance. The court will look upon a question asked by the party not to make this a ping-pong game or something like that. So it is always a question decided upon by the court. If this question raised is of any relevance, then the court will be prepared to allow it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms Residovic? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I am coming from a civil legal system, and in order to contribute to the ruling as best I can, I will tell you what the rules and procedures are in our legal system. The rule 89 of the rules of this Tribunal clearly points that if there are certain shortcomings in the rules, that the rules of procedures will be followed that are in accordance with the general rules and statute of the Tribunal. According to the legal system that is prevalent in the territory and now in the countries of all systems that have come out of Yugoslavia, there is examination and cross-examination, and last questioning belongs to the defence. Clearly the Trial Chamber implements the rules and can decide whether one of the parties is abusing their rights, and can rule that some questions may not be asked, but the right of the accused to ask the last questions is the basis of our legal system. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that all we have in terms of contributions, because it is open? Let us get everything before we decide what the interpretation of these rules are and what is happening in terms of the jurisdiction of the Tribunal in conformity with the international practice. This is what we want to make sure, because I do not want to conclude here and still find there is still grudging elements. I just want to know where we stand. I was quite amazed by the attitude, the approach adopted, but I know in litigation you can have anything. It is not new. You do not have to be amazed for that. It is common. There are certain interpretations one finds commonplace. Okay. In the absence of any more contributions we will give a ruling in the afternoon. We will have to consider it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for entertaining the motion. I appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we now have the witness for this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (In interpretation): I wish you a good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you remind him that he is still on oath?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am reminding you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. MR MIRKO KULJANIN (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Mr Kuljanin, yesterday we were talking about your stay in tunnel 9 when we interrupted our hearing. Let us go back then to that time and particularly to right after the very first night you spent in tunnel 9. Did anything particular happen the following morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing in particular except that they called us out. Some had more injuries than others that were visible. Those were mostly on the head, the face. Then we were called out so that we would be given some help, that would be bandaged and such. Nothing much beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Where were you brought for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went there towards the gate in that building there. There were some people there. I think that they were like nurses or something. They put some band aids on my head. Then I was returned with several others.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Were there many other persons from tunnel 9 brought there for the same reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that many. The one Mrkajic, whose eyes were shut, and I saw several more. There weren't that many. There were some who had head injuries when I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Was that in the morning of May 27?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Were you brought back to the tunnel right after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was returned there.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Now, during your stay in tunnel 9 did you have any occasion to see any mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no occasion to see, but on that same day, 27th, another group from Bradina was brought in. It was from the area called the Upper Bradina. They were beaten against that wall for five or six hours, and you could hear the screams and crying. There were people who suffered there. I was not there, but I found out about it later. One person, Slobo Vicic, was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. He said he found out about it later. He was not testifying from personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No, he is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I object to no personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, you said you heard screamings and noises coming from outside in that day, 27th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately what time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere after 12, afternoon, and it went on until the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: So do you mean that that kind of screaming and noises lasted during hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several hours, five, six hours maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe in detail this kind of noises and screaming you heard during that time, that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People were wailing and they were saying: "Don't! Don't!"; mostly screams, and wailing and begging not to be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did you hear that from inside tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only from within.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: In your opinion did these screamings and noises come from an area close from the tunnel entrance or far away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you asking his opinion or asking for fact? Are you asking for an opinion or asking for a fact? I do not think he is an opinion witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Since we are talking about what he has heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him from where the noises were coming. Why are you asking "your opinion"? Ask him from where the noises were coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know where the noises came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those noises and screams were coming from outside, from the direction of that wall, from that side, because none of us could see. We only heard that. That lasted several hours, five, six hours, depending on how long some of them endured.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Could you later have any occasion to find out what was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later, yes, when we met with these people, when I was transferred from Number 9 to Number 6, I found those people there, and they were talking about it, that they were standing there for a long time against the wall with their hands up, that they were beating them, and we heard all that is correct but we never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: So can you say who were these people?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. So were these people brought into tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not brought to Number 9. They wouldn't even fit there. Later when I was moved to Number 6, I saw them there. They were taken straight to Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to your stay in tunnel 9, was any prisoner called out by anybody while you were in tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that anybody was called out from Number 9 while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you stay in any other building, in any other place inside the Celebici camp besides tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After four or five days -- I don't know how long -- I was no longer in the Number 9. I was transferred then -- the whole group was transferred to Number 6. When another group arrived, then all of us went to Number 6, and this group was put into Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you give a description of hanger 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could, yes. It's a larger -- it's a larger tin hangar. I think it was used for some kind of garage. I don't know the exact length and width, but there was quite a bit of space there. I think that among the structures there I think that Number 6 was the biggest.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember how many doors did hangar 6 have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there was a double door from the one side. I don't know if they were on both ends and in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: But how many doors were normally used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One door at the end. At the entrance there was one door there, and occasionally it would be opened when somebody would come in and when people went out to have something to eat. Several at a time they would eat. We had some kind of vessel and a couple of spoons or bowls. When we would finish, the others would come. So one door was used for that, and when we asked to go out, sometimes when we needed to relieve ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did hangar 6 have any window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall it having windows, no. No, it did not have windows.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: How was light or darkness inside hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no light. In night-time it was dark and day-time you could see, but there was no light, at least while I was there. I was there for a short period, down there.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Anyway, some daylight could come inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, around the door there was a little bit, and maybe that tin -- I don't know, so you could see during day-time, so one could move about as much as one was allowed to, for instance when you went out.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Could you give any other more detailed description of the physical characteristics of building 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there were pillars. It was -- they were metal, and then there was tin, and I think that tin was also on the top and on the sides, and there were three doors on both ends and in the middle. That's how it looked. It already started being hot there from that tin, because it was quite hot.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, how long did you stay in building Number 6, in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not there a long time. I stayed there a short time. I don't know if you call it luck or not. Maybe luckily I think I stayed there four or five days and then I was transferred to Musala in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did every prisoner have a given position inside hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember that I had a specific spot. It was near the middle of the hangar, looking from the entrance door to the left, that middle door, and I know that that middle door sort of was interfering with my sitting, so that's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Maybe to be more clear may I ask that the witness be provided with Prosecution Exhibit number 1, page 7? Can it be placed either on the computer or on the ELMO? Maybe on the computer. Page 7 is map 5 right at the beginning of the booklet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this referring to Number 6?

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Could you point out your position inside hangar 6 on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Actually there were four rows. Where are the rows here? It does not show the rows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This should be the entrance door, as far as I recall. I was near the middle, and this is where the door was that is marked. Somewhere around the middle is where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you describe, indicate on this map how were the other prisoners distributed inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a circle around. When we arrived there already was no space to sit around, because people were sitting there. So then we filled in the rest of that space, I mean, next to the outer wall, and then a group started forming that was sitting in the middle. They could not -- we could not all fit against the wall to sit there, so two rows down the middle were formed, and people were sitting in the middle of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: All right. For the record, I would like the witness to be provided with a photocopy of this map so that a mark might be done on this photocopy, pointing out exactly for the record the position he had inside the hangar. Could you mark with a pen the position in which you were inside the hangar? Maybe we could put that on the ELMO just to have everybody appreciate it. Okay. Now if there is no objection, I would like this photocopy to be entered as exhibit, I believe, number 82?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We have no objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Then it is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, from your position, which you have been pointing out, could you see outside of the door of the hangar when the door was open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not see anything, because I was on a site where the door would open, and I couldn't see anything down there.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Could you see how were the general conditions of life in hangar Number 6? We start, for instance, with drinking water. How was the drinking water supplied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Water was the biggest problem, I guess, down there. I don't know what they used. I think that there was a bucket or some other tin vessel or something, and some of the prisoners I guess went -- the ones who served us -- so they would arrive, and those down there say: "Well, we have not got anything", so they would have to go again. So that was the problem. The problems were with water. The ones who had had the drink would ask again for some water, and you couldn't always get as much as you wanted and as much as you needed.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: What about food in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as food is concerned, it would arrive in front of the hangar. There was a crate there. They would -- there would be a pot or something, and then there were two or three spoons, and those who would come out first, it would be some kind of order that people were coming out, and they would take a few spoonfuls and a bit of bread, and then again the next with the same spoons, and so it was going around until everybody's turn came. I don't know if everybody would come to have their turn, but there were just a few spoonfuls.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the, let us say, sleeping facilities? Where did you sleep? How did you sleep inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In hangar Number 6 it was more comfortable, so that one could stretch. So sleeping -- so if a person who fall asleep -- there was a lot of opening of the door at night, so everybody was anxious that -- there was a lot of uncertainty as to what would happen. So that was sort of sleep, but there was not much.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any blankets or mattresses or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't have anything. I didn't have anything. I just had a shirt and a pair of trousers, and there was no access to any visitors, but also up there everything had been burnt, so there was nothing to be brought to us. I remember once some people had more blankets. Somebody in the hangar tore up these blankets and had given it to us, who had nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, could you please tell the court how were the toilet facilities during your stay in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no conditions. You had to ask a lot until you were permitted to go out. They would let two or three people out at a time. So the conditions were not good, because they rarely accommodated people. There were people who needed to go out more, and they didn't dare insist very much, because of the beatings. It was not simple to ask based on one's needs, but we did go out, and I did not notice that anybody relieved themselves inside, at least while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Where was the place where you used to -- which you used as a toilet while you were in hangar 6? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Left of the entrance there was something dug up. It was a ditch or something, and we went there to relieve ourselves, around the corner of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately how many prisoners were with you in hangar 6 in those days you remained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time somewhere around 200, at the time when I was there. Later I heard that more people arrived, but while I was there that was about the number.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did you see any of these prisoners with visible traces of mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How shall I put it? When I came to Number 6 a man unknown to me was on a crate at the entrance on the other side, and he lay motionless, and I did not know him, and he stayed there. Then I also noticed that Pero Mrkajic moved with difficulty, who also died there, but later I had gone by then. People had their own pain. Nobody was not beaten. Some of them were all right at that time, but suffered later, and I could not say about that, because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, you saw Pero Mrkajic inside hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Is that a different Mrkajic, Pero, than the one you saw in Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a different one. He is an elderly man and the one in Musala was a younger man. This is an elderly man who owned an restaurant in Bradina. He was older than I was. He died later, but at that time he had difficulty moving.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Was this Pero Mrkajic you saw in hangar 6 from Upper Bradina or from Lower Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was from Lower Bradina. He had a restaurant in the centre. I don't know what to call it. It was the centre of the village. There's always a centre in any kind of settlement, and that's where he had his restaurant and his house.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: When you arrived into hangar 6, did you recognise any of the prisoners coming from Upper Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew most of them. Maybe I didn't know the names of some of the younger ones, but I knew most of them by sight and even by name. I did know them.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to, say, approximately how many prisoners you found in hangar 6 coming from Upper Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were about 100 of them. I think that they were brought in on the 27th. Their village is larger than ours, and I think that there were about 100 of them. There were some others there whom I did not know from other villages in the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you give us a description of the physical conditions of any of these prisoners you recognised as coming from Upper Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were quite a few of them who complained of more serious injuries, but all of them were able to move. They did not have any head injuries. I heard from them that they were told, when they were brought in and beaten, that the instruction was for them not to be beaten on the head.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did any of them receive any medical care, as far as you know, during your stay in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about any of them having died?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is asking a question that calls for speculation on his part; if he saw someone die, that is another thing. If he heard about it from other people -- if he asked if he saw them, that would be a more appropriate question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question like that: did you see any dead person belonging to the group of Upper Bradina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Where? In hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In hangar Number 6, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, did you ever see any of the guards coming to hangar 6 while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They did come and talk to us. We went out to have something to eat. We were taken out into the compound. Then if we had to go out to relieve ourselves, but I did not know anyone of the guards, but they did carry out their tasks, but there was no structure like that at the time when I was there for the four days. In that brief period I was not able to see much. Only one evening there was one occasion Radoslav Kuljanin was called out, and I left the day after that. He was taken out in front of the hangar and we could hear the beating and the screams and the moaning. He was brought in next to the door, and then I left and he stayed there lying down. That is the only thing that I heard. I couldn't see who it was, because he had been taken out. Even if I had seen the people who beat them, because I couldn't -- I didn't know them, because I knew very few people from Konjic, especially the younger ones.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, do you know the names of any of the guards you might have seen?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already answered that. He does not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If he found out after the fact, it is not relevant to this proceeding. It is whether he knew them at that time and could he recognise them then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you please clarify what is this all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already answered he did not know the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My question was did he know any name of guards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already said that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is what I said. I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, do you know who was the Commander of the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't vouch for the identity of the person. I don't have personal knowledge, but in the few days I was there I couldn't learn that much, but I can tell you that I did meet somebody there who was apparently in charge. He had a bandage on his foot or leg, and he was walking on crutches in the few days I was there, but I did not know who that person was at the time. I learned later that it was somebody by the name of Delic. Then when I went to Konjic, that's when I learned. I learned that from the people who knew him in Konjic, but again I can't say that I could see -- say I saw him participate in anything. That's only -- the only thing I heard was that somebody called this Kuljanin out and that he was beaten there.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: You mean Radoslav?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the three or four days. Yes, that is correct, Radoslav Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: How frequently did you see Mr Delic inside Celebici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said he had not seen him. He has already answered that question. He has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: He did say he saw him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He saw a man on crutches and later on he learned what his name was. In the camp he did not know he was the commander. That is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How frequently did you see this person with some problem of the legs during your stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the three or four days that I was there, in Number 6, I saw him every day.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Was he using crutches every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw him, he was on crutches while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say what he came -- what did he come for to hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really say what his duties were, but from what I saw he had a say in things. I think maybe he was even in charge of the cutting up of the blankets and the distribution of those blankets. It is possible. It's very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, were you ever interrogated by military investigators during your stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Were you still in tunnel 9 or already in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Where in the camp did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Down there towards the entrance gates there was an administration building there, a command building to the left. I think there was a porch there on that building. This is where a man sat and questioned people. There were two of them there. I think he was dressed in civilian clothes. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Were you accused of anything specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not accuse me of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of this person who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I spent a very brief time there. I don't know if he continued to discharge that duty after I left. I don't know, but I did not see him after that, and then I left.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: How did this man treat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that the treatment was not bad. He told me that I should say everything. It wasn't a bad experience.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Was that a long interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember what did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The thing that I remember best is that he asked me whether I had weapons, and I responded truthfully. As for the other things, he accused me of some things and then I had to respond to the allegations, but they didn't last long.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, may I mark a document for identification as exhibit number 83 and 83A? May I ask that the original be put on the ELMO for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What are these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is the statement given to this -- during this interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: By?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: By the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The officer -- you can read out the statement to him. Does it bear his signature or anything of that sort? Read out the statement and ask him whether he made the statement or not. Then only can you have it exhibited. How does he know what this statement is?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If you may, I am quite confused. We are not aware of what statement this is they are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is what I want to find out. The statement can be read out to the witness and he can say this is the statement he made before the officer who interrogated him in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I do not know. I would like to know that too. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Unless you read out the statement, how would he know it is a statement he made?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Well, Mr Kuljanin, do you remember having signed a statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: First, read it out and ask him whether he signed it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. I know that I did not read this. I don't know if it includes all the words that I said, but I know that I didn't stay there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is disowning the statement, so how can you have it exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I would like this statement in original to be shown to the witness on the ELMO and my question is: do you recognise this piece of paper for any detail on it, and particularly do you recognise as yours the signature appearing on the bottom of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the signature. The signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember having said to the person who interrogated some details about rifles received by Slobodan Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are you referring to this statement or are you referring to some other fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Read out the statement to him. Ask him whether he has made this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I can read out the statement in English, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will have a break now and come back at 11.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr Turone, are you all right to carry on now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, your Honour. Coming back to this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please hold on. I think -- MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, during the break a problem in the treatment of our clients occurred, and I would like to ask your permission to present this problem now before this part of the hearing is concluded, so that maybe you can make an appropriate ruling on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. Let us clear up this matter and know what exactly the position is. What is the problem? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, during one of the status conferences we presented the problem of the transport of the accused to the court room, and we indicated that these problems will increase during the trial, because our clients spend the time during the early morning until the late evening here, and that we indicated that it might cause problems for them following the trial, and it is of vital importance for all four of them. When we were preparing for this trial during the induction course that we attended together with the Registry, all of us defence counsel, when we were asked whether we want to be in touch with our clients during every break, we said "yes", and we asked that we be allowed to be in touch with our clients during the lunch break and also during all the other breaks in the proceedings during the day. However, ever since the first day there have been problems. Depending on the security guards' shifts, our clients are either allowed to get out during the break or they are not allowed to leave the court room, and the explanation is that there are technical problems. Allegedly they cannot take four people out in the period of 20 minutes. Your Honours, I think that this violates the basic rights of our clients to have a brief break during the daily proceedings, and I already said that it is long for us, but it is even longer for them, because the transportation takes at least two hours. Thus they are unable to talk to us. They are not able to smoke a cigarette or have a coffee, and that engenders unnecessary and I think unpermissible problems to us and to our clients, and on the other hand, I think it could also cause problems for this Tribunal, because they cannot be concentrated to follow the presentation of evidence. Therefore, I would like to ask you, your Honours, to make a ruling which would enable them to use every break that we have, and that our clients are enabled to leave the court room during those breaks and to be in contact with their defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before -- may I say I few things? I think counsel have a right to have free access to their clients during the trial and a ruling should be made that they can meet them and talk to them during the breaks. You should have free access to your clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is a technical problem, as you have mentioned, and especially -- perhaps the Trial Chamber might not take a decision without conferring with the security about how these arrangements can be done, but I think we will immediately try to get in touch with them and find out how we can ameliorate these problems, because I know everyone is uneasy as to how long one can stay without this type of freedom. I think we will try to see what we can do. At least by the close of the day we will tell you what we have agreed upon. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you very much, your Honour. If the problem is in the duration of the break, I know you will make it longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: As I said, by the end of the day we will try to see how to adjust it so that it might make things easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the side of the prosecution -- I just want to bring to your Honour's attention from the side of the prosecution we support these suggestions by the defence counsels, and we defer this question to your Honours and to the Registrar to find a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr Ostberg. As I indicated, these are not decisions you take arbitrarily. You have to get those particularly involved. Thank you very much. Mr Turone, you can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So coming back to this document, which was anyway shown to the defence before this hearing, my idea was to mark that for identification and put it on the ELMO for the witness to identify that, but I understand that you prefer, your Honour, that I read it in English translation and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If he can read it himself, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please, when you have a question of a statement you want to tender, you have a way of getting the witness to admit he made such a statement. When he has admitted making the statement, you show it to him and he can read it. If it is his statement, then you tender it. You do not have to read it. He can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. This is what exactly I proposed to do. Mr Kuljanin, if you can look at this document on your right hand, can you read it and say whether you recognise this as a statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you I can't remember what statements I gave, but I can confirm that this is my signature. That is true. I don't know if I could read all this. I have problems seeing, but if I can read this and if I notice something that I remember that had been added -- I know very well that nothing was read to me after the questioning. I signed because I was not in any condition to say that I don't want to sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: But you made a statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You made a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But he is only admitting the signatures. He is not admitting its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a different matter. You made a statement. Perhaps if you know this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise my signature, but I do not know what is in the statement because I was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, could you please read this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot read it. I would prefer if somebody would read it for me, because I really have problems seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Of course you can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not everything is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: -- read it not on the screen, but the real piece of paper you have on the table beside you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Maybe we could solve this problem more expeditiously if the court is aware the defence has no objections to the admission of this statement into evidence by the prosecution. The only thing that we do have one objection to is that there is an interpretation to English by the prosecution, and there is an interpretation into English by the interpreters, and there is a discrepancy between the interpretation. As far as the original document, we have no objection. It might assist Mr Turone right now in his endeavours to try to get it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms McMurrey.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So our position would be to tender this document as exhibit number 83 and have the English translation reviewed further on, if there is no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Since it is an admitted document, it may be exhibited. Since this is an admitted document, let it be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: There is a simple way. He has admitted he made a statement. The signature is his own. So you can tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. I tender this exhibit as exhibit 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If possible, let it be read out so that the interpreters will read it, so he will know exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean the interpreter should read it out in the original language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, and it will be interpreted. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, we agree that this is the document. We would just like to point out some discrepancies in the translation. The translation of a sentence here is missing, indicating that during the inspection he carried a weapon and Rajko had a semi-automatic rifle. There is also another part of a sentence missing saying that the men that he had warned to hand over their weapons did not agree to do so. This is not incorrectly translated. Finally, there is an introduction to this statement, which does not exist in the original. I think that the interpreters can now make an -- all the appropriate corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The interpretation is not in evidence now so it is not part of the document tendered. When the interpreters interpret it, that will be sufficient for the interpretation of the statement he made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Give us an agreed translation, so there is no particular difficulty. You can translate it and show it to the defence. They agree to it and file. The document is this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My proposal is that the agreed translation may be handed over later on because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: There is no translation before us now. There is none now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We have now a translation, and it is a translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Which is disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Which is disputed, because there are some words which were not legible enough in the opinion of the interpreter who did this translation which is now disputed. Now the possibilities in my opinion are two: either -- whether we might have the original read out to the witness, or we might decide that this disputed translation be read out in English. I don't see any other possibility right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Why do you want to read out the disputed interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is not what I mean to do. I think my proposal is to have the original read out in Serbian language by somebody, but this cannot be me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be of assistance to the court, that we have a translation here that we feel is accurate. If the prosecution will agree to this right now, then we could distribute it. We have copies and we could all go on with this evidence, or Ms Residovic could read it in the language of Bosnian, and it can be interpreted for you on the headsets at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This can be a good possibility in our opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Whatever you choose. We have an English translation and we have Ms Residovic, who reads the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let counsel read it out. He will be listening. If he does not agree with it, he will say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please read it out very slowly, Ms Residovic. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I would just like the witness to react if I read anything that is not accurate, because I cannot say anything about the truth of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: All you are reading is his statement. Where it is not agreed to him, he will say so. So read it exactly without any annotation or without even any embellishment of it. Just read his statement. Let the interpreter interpret it. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): The heading is: "Republic BiH, Municipality of Konjic, TO and HVO Headquarters, Municipal Headquarters, Konjic. Date: 2nd June 1992". Then on one side, on the upper side, there is the marking "3K". "Record. Drawn up on 2nd June 1992 on the premises of the TO and HVO headquarters, Konjic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: "Kuljanin Mirko, son of Milan and Savka" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not Konjic, Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: -- "Gligorevic, 23rd October 1931, Bradina, residing in Bradina, retired. I am not a member of the SDS, although I had been offered to join the party. I received a weapon two months ago from Slobodan Kuljanin an M-48 rifle, and 45 rounds. Fifteen days ago I was assigned with Rajko Kuljanin to go to Velika and to patrol it. On that occasion I carried the weapon and Rajko had a semi-automatic rifle. Our neighbours met us in Velika, our neighbours from Repocin, with Hamzo Ajanovic. We spoke for a while and they told us to leave the rifles, and we did accordingly. We did not resist this. We advised the people in Bradina about that and we told them to hand over the weapons, which they did not agree to do. They offered me weapons again, but I refused to accept it, I had a pistol with a permit, which I handed over when I surrendered. When the fighting started, I was with my wife and children in the basement. We surrendered the same day. I have a son whose name is Novica, and he had an AP automatic rifle. I don't know what happened to him. Statement given by Mirko Kuljanin. Statement taken by Mladen Zovko."

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, did you hear what was read out right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard, but it does not correspond to the truth. I did not go on any patrols. I just went with this man to plant potatoes. I went to my plot of land, and we had no intention of trespassing or going in any other -- to any other village. I do not know what it says here, that he carried a PAP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is your son has an AP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but what about Rajko?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: PAP is semi-automatic rifle, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard somebody say "PAP, P-A-P", but I thought it was a larger weapon, as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: But is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, but there are some words that have been added, but he didn't read it to me, and I was in no condition to ask for it to be read to me, but there are some questions and my answers. The signature is mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Which bits have been added?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That they were captured, that has been added; that I was told to surrender the weapons, that has also been added; that Ajanovic, that has also been added. I know only that they said that there was some commander there, and I thought that this Ajanovic -- he used to be an active serviceman. I mentioned his name and they said "yes". This is what this was all about, but Ajanovic was not there at the time. There were seven or eight other people. I think I knew about two of them by sight, but I did not know their names. They took the weapons away with them. They were armed themselves. Everybody was armed, and I just said: "I don't know why you think -- what would have happened if we continued going towards your village? You can see we just went to work our land. If I had went any further towards your village, towards your property, I would have agreed to you killing me, but we didn't do that. We just went to our land, to our property."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Now, Mr Kuljanin, could you tell us approximately when did you leave Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think soon thereafter, after -- I think two or three days after I gave this statement, because if I hadn't given the statement if this formality hadn't been taken, I heard that there would be some transfers, and if no statement had been given, no transfer would be done, and we heard that the conditions in Konjic were better, and since I was an elderly man and there were no allegations, charges against me, I managed to be questioned as required and I managed to be transferred, maybe on 3rd or 4th June, thereabouts. I don't know exactly. I don't remember the exact date, but I think that my total stay there was about ten days, both in Number 6 and in Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: You mean the total number of days in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. Another correction. This was not made in Konjic but in Celebici, in the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Correct,. Celebici is inside the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, you said: "I was transferred." Where were you transferred exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, from Celebici --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how large the group was, but a group was transferred to the sports hall in Konjic, in Musala, and I stayed there until I was released, until I was let go.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you explain in more detail how was this transfer carried on? Who called you out of hangar 6 in order to be transferred to Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could describe that the way I know it. Some people arrived and I think that there were some people in charge. They came into the hangar. They walked around. They pointed fingers to separate people. I don't know who these people were, but I was separated out, among others, and I came out, and they transferred us in a van to Konjic, in the sports hall in Konjic at Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: How many prisoners were with you in the van going from Celebici to Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the exact number. Maybe at that time maybe ten or fifteen. I don't know. I don't know exactly how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Musala sports hall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there until I was released from the camp. I think that was on 24th, 25th -- 24th August.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know who was the Commander of the Musala camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Musala I can say that I noticed that Pavo would show up, that he was respected there, but I know that he did not come very often, but when he did, he was given respect. Now who was the real Commander of all these camps, that I don't know. Whether it was separated, whether there was one Commander, and such things.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know the full name of this Pavo you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be Zdravko Mucic, as far as I know, called Pavo, and I only met him when I was transferred to Konjic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: How frequently did you see him in Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very often. As I said, he would show up. Not very often, but we sensed because there was all kind of order and the people were telling us to get up, things like that, but he did not show up very often. I was there a bit longer. I can say that he appeared daily maybe once a week, not often, no.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: When you arrived at Musala, coming from Celebici, did anybody in charge of that camp, of Musala, register your names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't. Maybe there was a list somewhere about who was there, but I don't know about it. What I can describe is that shortly after I arrived I was in a room which was called Number 6. Number 6, there were locker rooms, and it was over 30 of us. It was quite packed, and later I was transferred to Number 8, and I stayed there until I was released.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any occasion of seeing Mr Mucic while you were in the first place inside Musala?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said that he used to come once a week maybe. He must have seen him. He has already said that is correct that he used to come once a week. He must have seen him. Why are you asking how frequently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I would like him to say which was the first time when he saw Mr Mucic in Musala camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really think that what he is trying to do is have a little bit of cross-examination of his own witness, with respect. He has done very well so far, but I think he is straying into that realm and I would ask that he perhaps just be careful about that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean this is a leading question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, I meant it was a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are cross-examining a statement he already made. You are cross-examining him really. He said that. Fair enough. Proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are in agreement, your Honours, I could say that when he would come, this Zdravko Mucic, he came when we were in that big hall, and I did not notice him. I did not see him coming to these small rooms when they were there. I did not see him there. He would only come to the door in the big room where we were sitting around in that sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Mr Kuljanin, did you ever have occasion of seeing in Musala any of the guards being in charge in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. He already said he did not know any of the guards in Celebici and he could not identify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What he is asking is whether he at any time saw any of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: From Celebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe they were common guards. Maybe he can say some persons he saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He is not talking about knowing them. It is whether he saw any of them. It is quite a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Did he see any of the guards from Celebici was the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. He did not have to know them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said he did not know the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You do not have to know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you understand my question, Mr Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall and from the people who knew, I saw this man called Zenga. I saw him twice. I must say that I didn't get anything from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this testimony. The exact statement was "from people who knew". He is not using his own personal knowledge about the name of this person, and he is testifying from no personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, if somebody points out another person to you and tells you "this is this man", you know he could still use that. That is knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe he was not testifying from personal knowledge. It is only what somebody else told him. We have no way of authenticating whether that person knew this person or not, and it is hearsay, but it is more than that. It is unreliable testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, it might be when your cross-examination goes to make it totally unreliable, because he does not claim to have known him himself. Somebody told him about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Apart from that, you are assessing the probative value at this stage. The evidence comes and then we can find out how much probative value it has.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let it come in. This is how he got to know who he said this man was. When you challenge him about his knowledge, you might show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could also object as to the relevancy of this whole line. The questioning makes no fact of importance to the indictment more or less likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are a little unfamiliar with our rules. All it says, if it is relative or probative, I suppose this is going to that extent. You still have a chance of destroying whatever the basis for that knowledge is. You still have a chance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Apart from that, I think counsel is right saying we are more concerned with what happened at Celebici rather than Musala.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We would like to join in Mr Moran's objection that what happened at Musala is irrelevant to these proceedings also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Anyway, your Honour, I am going to tender the release form of this witness, and the release form for this witness has a signature of one of our defendants. This release form was done, of course, after the detention period in Musala. So there is a sort of linkage between the two periods. This is why in my opinion we cannot say that whatever happened in Musala is not relevant to our trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Put to him the release order straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am arriving to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Might I suggest the more appropriate way would be to question him from the release order that he intends to put into evidence, and then we are not led astray with irrelevant situations that may or may not have occurred at Musala. That is our objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I say is that the relevance of some questions can be appreciated after some other questions which might come later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know. The type of anticipation you are going about may make matters more difficult for you. Sometimes you allow the evidence to come in, so that you know what to do. Now you are anticipating a thing which you cannot really defend. If he has a discharge certificate, obviously it is a discharge certificate from the witness, which necessarily must come in. He wants this chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We agree. Let us put it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What are you arguing about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The other irrelevant things he was questioning about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Has he said anything more than that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The discharge certificate?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe the original question was something else, but we agree wholly with his putting that in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The discharge certificate, let us carry on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: On the other hand, your Honours, our evidence will show in our opinion that Mr Mucic was in charge of both Celebici and Musala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is nothing to do with this witness. It is nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Go on. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So how did you get to know this name, Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
