utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. This is completely objectionable and irrelevant, what he found out at Musala, to what happened at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The question is: how did you know the name Zenga? What is objectionable about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Because he found out at Musala way after the fact. It has nothing to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not why he could not have known about the name Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is irrelevant to the period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: How is it irrelevant? Can he not know the name? How much he knew it is what he is being asked about. Let him state how he knew it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The answer is somebody else told him, I am sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Has he said so?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, but that is unreliable testimony. So ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Would you answer to my question, Mr Kuljanin? How did you get to know this name "Zenga"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, because I can't be sure, but at least twice I know that he came and saw the rooms, and I remember him having some white belt on him, and the word, I think, spread that somebody had bad experiences with him so --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to object to that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do not waste our time. Let him give his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He is talking about what somebody else said about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I said leave him to give his evidence. You have no right to give evidence for him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that I found out about him that way, and as far as direct contact with me, no, I did not know him, but through that -- but twice I know, I am sure 100 per cent, he came down the hallway and looked into every room, and one could see that he was looking for something or someone. I don't know what, but the people who knew him were not happy to meet with him. Why? We know why. Those who were threatened by him know that best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So my next question is: how do you know he was a Celebici guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am in a position to know, because people were transferred back and forth quite a bit, so that a lot was known and a lot was -- even though it was a camp, it was a prison. Somehow you find out about things, but those who were eye-witnesses, they know, but the others also gained knowledge somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Now, Mr Kuljanin, when you were released from Musala camp, who called you for releasing you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The direct calling out I don't know, but I know that I got into a van, which took me to Donje Selo. I had limited movement for Donje Selo and Celebici. I think that's what should be in my release order, "limited movement", but at that time, we were driven by Pavo Mucic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Driven in the van, you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Could you tell us more details on this -- on how and from whom you received this release form you have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if it was given out by the same person, these release forms. I could not guarantee that, but all of us who came out that day, who were released, we all got those release forms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Who gave you your release form? Who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether it was Mucic or someone else, but from what I could see it was his signature on it and also I don't recall who called me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You do not recall who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether it was that same Pavo or someone else, but I received it in my hands. I know that he drove us to Donje Selo. That I know, when we were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Now, your Honour, I would like to have this document marked for identification as number 84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just before you do that, did Mucic sign the release order in your presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No it had been prepared beforehand, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So I would like to have this marked for identification as Exhibit Number 84 and 84A for the English translation. This is also the document which we prepared for the convenience of your Honours, and defence counsel has it already, as far as I know. Could we please place the original language form on the ELMO? Mr Kuljanin, can you recognise this document? Is that familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I received when I left camp. Yes, that's what I received.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: So can you say to whom the signature belongs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not legible enough to me but as far as I can make it out, it says "Mucic".

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. The date of this release form, can you read the date of this release form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see. 26th you say? No. No, that's when I was arrested. I am sorry. I have difficulty finding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is this in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am perfectly happy that my learned friend should direct the witness' attention to the place where the date is to be found. It seems sensible to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If I am allowed to do that without that being a leading question, I would say this is on top of the paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: 19th August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, up there. 19th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So, your Honours, if there are no objections, I would like to tender Exhibit Number 84 for admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We have no objections, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Admitted. Coming to the end, I would like now the witness to look at the video we have been looking at already a couple of days ago. It is exhibit D1-2 of the defence. I would like to ask Mr Kuljanin, whether he recognises anybody in this video. Mr Kuljanin, you tell us if you recognise people in this video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise myself and Djorde Milan. I recognise myself; Djorde Milan; Gligorevic. I can't recall the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say in which place was the videotape done? Do you remember the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- I recall the name, Mitar Gligorevic. That I don't know. I couldn't tell you when this was filmed and who did it, and whether that was the date. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: I mean, my question is: do you recognise the place in which the videotape was -- in which you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could it have been in the sports hall? I couldn't quite tell you. If it wasn't there, then I don't know where it was. This is -- Boro Kuljanin it looks, and Mrkajic Mijailo. Then it couldn't be in Konjic. I see Mrkajic Mijailo. Samoukovic Simo, I see him up there, and the Gligorevic fellow. That's me. This is myself.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: All right, your Honour. My examination-in-chief is finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I asked to take that cap with me so I could put it on, because of the injuries I had on my head, and they allowed me that. This is Milan Djordjic, who was the oldest in the camp. He was 73 years old at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR TURONE
utterances.text: I have no more questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is just one thing I want to find out. This video is prepared on the afternoon of 20th August, as the date and the time shows. The release order is 19th August. So it must be -- the release order is issued in Konjic. It must be after he has been released these photographs were taken. I just want to find out information. The release order is 19th August?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This video is done on --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This video is done on 20th August. I had some question, but he did not have a real precise answer, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose it might depend on when he actually left the place. It could have been signed on 19th August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He might have not left then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: To our question he replied he is not sure about the exact day of the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: There is a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr Kuljanin, yesterday you told the court that the day you were arrested there was a group of women and children. That was in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bradina, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Would you tell the court, if you know, where this group was taken out, this group of women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can tell that. They were separated out at that intersection centre. They were separated to one side, and we were lined up on the road leading towards Konjic. Women and children were separated out to the right of us and then they were taken to that elementary school in Bradina. That's where the women and children were taken, and also my father was there. For me it was very important. He was 84 years old. He was beaten up, and he was in pain for two days and then he died. I don't know if he was any soldier, but I mentioned that everything was going to be destroyed that day; they went to destroy it. That's what they did. That same date, the 26th, over 20 people were killed in that hamlet, in that village, and through all this time -- by the time I completed my stay in the camps, 60 per cent were killed from Bradina. This is what I know. I could not have been an eye-witness, but I am not insane either. We survived it, contact and meet. So in that way we found all that out. There is a common grave near the church in Bradina and 17 or 18 victims were buried in there. I don't know what happened to that common grave. I don't know if it's still there or not. Then others were buried, the ones who came later, in that same churchyard. Some were buried in the cemetery as well. I don't know in what shape all that is now. I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. So these women and children were also arrested and mistreated? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They had to undergo various things. Women and girls were taken out during the night and again this is what we managed to find out when we talked among ourselves. I was not an eye-witness to that. That's because I was taken to the Konjic and Celebici camps. Another thing, a few houses were left standing until 12th July, and then a new operation was conducted and everything was razed to the ground, and while we were still in the camp some people were saying that we would be allowed to go back to our homes, to our property, but some people didn't want that. Some people did not want us to go back to our homes, and so they finished the job on 12th or 13th July. That was the time when my father, who remained at home with my wife and daughter-in-law, and my grandchildren -- that's when he was killed, at the age of 84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr Kuljanin,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness is on for cross-examination now, but I don't know. It depends. We have only ten minutes before we break for lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell you that I have no questions for this witness, so I think the next in line will have to answer your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I am next in line. Whatever the court's pleasure. If the court wants to break a little bit earlier, it is fine. If the court wants me to continue now and stop for a break; I don't have a lot of cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is that the agreed order of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you agreed the order in which the cross-examination will proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. We were to proceed with defence for Mr Mucic, Mr Delic, Mr Landzo and then Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court, Mr Kuljanin, my name is Tom Moran. I am one of the defence lawyers. I would like to ask you a few questions to clear some things up. If I ask you a question you don't understand, will you stop me and ask me to rephrase it. If you just listen to my question and just answer the question, I think this may go a little bit quicker. The first thing I would ask you is this: from your testimony yesterday and earlier today would it be fair to say that while you were -- between the time you were initially arrested and the time you arrived at Celebici was the time that the worst treatment occurred; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And that, in fact, once you arrived at Celebici, if there was any mistreatment, it was considerably less than it had been before you got there; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. Yes, considerably less, but I suffered the consequences from the injuries I sustained on my way to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: I understand that is correct sir, and I will get to that in a second. I will cover that with you. If I can talk about wanting to try to commit suicide with a nail right after you got to the camp -- remember that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: That was because of the treatment that you received from other people before you got to the camp that you were suicidal; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the way there.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: From your observations at the camp at Celebici for the time you were both in the tunnel and in the hangar, would it be right to characterise your testimony as there was a seeming lack of organisation among the staff of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because from what I was able to conclude everyone was left to their own devices, because it seemed that there was not enough care or command over the people who were thus enabled to do whatever they wanted to do. I think that their behaviour -- I think that human beings were not respected. Everybody just wanted to survive, and all of us in that group, we had no dignity.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, would it be fair to say the Celebici camp was really not designed to hold prisoners, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. It was somebody's intention, that's for sure. We were taken there, and on my way, while I was on my way to Celebici, I was not aware of its existence. I thought we would end up somewhere else in a different manner. I don't know. Maybe it would even have been better, and then when I left the group to hand over the pistol, maybe it would have been better for me to be finished there, but it's up to God.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: What I am getting at is: would it not be fair to say that the Celebici camp was originally designed to do something other than hold prisoners and it was being used to hold prisoners and being adapted for that purpose, even though it was not designed for that purpose. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the facilities were not built at that time, but somebody used them for that purpose. That is a known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct. So, for instance, in hangar Number 6 there was no plumbing there, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: And if people were going to bring water, if you were going to have to have anything to drink, people would have to bring water there, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I say there was no care for the survival of the people there. This is my conclusion based on my experience. After all, I survived that. There was lack of hygiene. We could not change our clothes. We couldn't wash. We all ate with the same spoon, 20 of us. We took turns using the same spoon and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not washed.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, there was a shortage of water around the whole area, was there not, drinking water, due to the war and the conditions brought on by the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I was able to notice, there was plenty of water from the wells, but there was water coming out of the wells, and we really had trouble getting water. We would have given anything for a drink of water, but we didn't have access to it, neither to drink any, nor to wash. Of course, drinking was the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: The way you described it either yesterday or this morning was people were bringing it in buckets of some kind, either tubs or buckets, some tin containers, to bring you water in hangar 6 on a fairly regular basis, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not really regularly, because the demand was such that they should have been bringing the water all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr Moran --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not enough water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: -- it is convenient to stop. So you can continue after lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will break and reassemble at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I have to clear up just two things before we continue with the witness: the question of the security and the comfort of the accused persons. We have agreed we should be able to have a break of 30 minutes to enable the accused persons to be taken down by the security. The perhaps more elaborate aspect, which is that -- which concerns the Dutch security, we have not been able immediately to solve, but later perhaps the Registrar will take that up and they will know how to deal with that. I think within the 30 minutes you should be able to communicate with your clients and not worry about it. The second thing is I said we would read a short ruling on the motion so that we will know what we are doing. You have been cross-examining and will continue to do so. The motion seeks an interpretation of Rule 85 of the rules of procedure in evidence. It was brought by counsel for the fourth accused, Esad Landzo. The interpretation contended for is that every submission of the witness must involve examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination, re-cross-examination. It is clear that this is the meaning of a combined reading of Rules 85A and B of our rules of procedure and evidence. Learned counsel submitted that the Trial Chamber has adopted such an interpretation, and criminal procedures of the United States, Canada and Scotland also adopt the same procedure. It has been argued that the failure of this Trial Chamber to do so places the accused persons at a disadvantage and prejudices their chances of a fair trial. Counsel relies on the provisions of Rule 21(4)(E) of the Tribunal's statute, which vests in the accused the right to examine or have examined the witnesses against him. It is also argued that there is a conflict between the practice of this Trial Chamber and the practice adopted during the Tadic trials. The contention of counsel was supported by other counsel, except counsel for Mr Mucic, the second accused. The ruling we are now reading is a summary of the decision, because we still have to write a reasoned decision later, because the Trial Chamber does intend to hand that down later. Just to bridge a gap while this problem is solved. It is a fundamental principle in the administration of justice that where a court has formulated rules to govern its proceedings, it is bound by the provisions of the rules so formulated. It is an elementary principle of the interpretation from which a departure is very rare and it is inherently dangerous that where the meaning of words used in a provision are clear and unambiguous, it should be given such meaning without any annotation. It is a rule from which the court seldom departs. Rule 85 is divided into two paragraphs, A and B. (Actually it is three, but the relevant portion is A and B.) Paragraph A deals with the order of presentation of evidence. Paragraph B is concerned with the examination of witnesses. Each paragraph is complete in itself and does not require paraphrasing for its application. The order of presentation of evidence is as stated in 1-5. The order for examining witnesses are stated in B. This is the general rule. In practice a court has always exercised a discretion in the interests of justice to allow further cross-examination of prosecution witnesses where the re-examination raises a new matter or where the interests of justice so requires. The Trial Chamber does not agree with the submission that the US, Canada and Scottish practice permits re-cross-examination as a matter of general rule. We are fairly aware of decided cases which make it an exception. The provisions of Rule 85B are clear and unambiguous and require no interpretation. We abide by that rule. This is our ruling on the matter. We still have examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination. If any new matter arises or if the interests of justice so require, further cross-examination can be allowed. We can then proceed to invite the witness, so that we can continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had offered to the Registrar earlier the videotape that we talked about yesterday during the cross-examination of Mr Gotovac. I think it is being marked, but I would like to offer it into evidence at this point, as we discussed, and it is the video that was shown yesterday in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I46 you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It was marked for prosecution identification purposes I46. I am sure it will now have a D something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Only the portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That was shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it accepted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr Turone, I just want to find out: the statement which this witness has made, is it in his own handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This statement which you supplied a copy of, is it in his own handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is in the copy which we have given --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: He recognised only the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please inform the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. Would it be more convenient for you to come over there so we can also see you? We cannot see you from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine, judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court, sir. Before lunch we were discussing some of the conditions at Celebici and how the camp really had not been designed to be a prison camp. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall, but my opinion is that there was this military installation there, but from what I had known before there had been some soldiers there, but they were gone, and then there was some news on TV from Grude about that. Somebody removed them from there so that they wouldn't interfere, so it is my opinion that somebody did it intentionally. There was an intention to do so even before the war broke out there.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, let me -- for instance, on the area of medical care, remember that you testified earlier that the day after you arrived and you spent the night in the tunnel that you were brought out for some medical care; do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't really any proper assistance. I just was given a band aid. I had two quite large wounds on my head that were cleaned there, and then they just covered those wounds. They did not apply any medication. I didn't get anything else. Excuse me. That's why I later asked them to be allowed to put the cap that I had found somewhere, to put it on my head.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Right, sir. I understand. When you were there in late May and early June, they had not set up an infirmary yet, had they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about an infirmary. I went to that building one morning, which was supposed to be the command building right there at the entrance. That's where I went, and that's where I was given the band aids. I don't know anything about any infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: That is right, sir. They were short of supplies, for instance blankets. Do you recall that some people had blankets and other people did not. Do you recall testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Do you recall, of course, testifying that a man that you identified as Hazim Delic collected blankets and cut them up and made sure that everybody had something for a blanket. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember very well, because we from Bradina, we arrived there practically naked, without coats, without hats, just in our shirt sleeves, let alone any blankets, and I know that there was this man -- there were several of them actually -- but I think that he was also among them, and that he did that.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: He was the man on crutches; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, when he was on the crutches, was he able to get around well, or did it appear that it was hard for him to move around because of his injury?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know really. Well, I had some difficulty. I couldn't really tell you exactly. I don't know what the matter was. I just know that he had a bandage on his leg and he was on crutches.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: When you were at Celebici was there any shelling or bombing of the camp or the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: How about when you were in the sports hall at Marsala? Was there any shelling there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I was there when two shells hit that place and 13 people were killed inside in the hall itself. I don't know where the shells had come from or what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: But it was a dangerous place to be, because it was in the middle of the war zone, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess. It was dangerous indeed. Wherever there is any shooting, it's dangerous, but there were no safety measures. It wasn't very safe there. There was just glass above on the roof, so it was very easy for the shells to hit the hall and they hit the wall, and when the wall crumbled, that's actually how those people got killed. It was even more harmful than the shells themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: A couple more questions, sir, and I believe I will be through. Before we started our cross-examination you were asked by one of the judges about the women and children who were arrested in Bradina with you; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Those women and children were never taken to Celebici, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were taken to Celebici, actually to Konjic. I saw some of them there, some of them who I knew. They were placed in room number 1, maybe five or six of them. They were there for a while and then they were released.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: That is Konjic, not Celebici; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know about those in Konjic. I don't know anything about the women in Celebici, because I was not there for a long time, and I don't know anything about that for the short time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, one other area of questioning, and before I start it, I do not want you to tell me where you reside now specifically; is that fair enough? I read in your statement and there was an indication that you are now a resident of the United States; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you really want him to answer this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, the follow-up is going to be I just want to know if anyone from the Tribunal or from the Office of the Prosecutor helped him gain his visa to live in the United States. If they did not, that is as far as I want to go, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Why do you need to ask that? It is unnecessary. As far as the prosecution is concerned, they protect this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That is why I do not want to know what it is specifically. If the court thinks it is irrelevant, I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, your Honour. With that I pass the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will not answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Who is it next for the witness? Yes, it is for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the court. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Dobodan, Mr Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: If the court would let me, I would just like to commend you. It is so refreshing to have a witness who listens to the question and responds in the manner you have done. I want just to commend you for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Now, I just have a few questions I would like to ask. Just for clarification, Mr Kuljanin, you did state that the worst torture and beating that you received was from Bradina to the tunnel, and I just want for clarification: that tunnel was the road tunnel outside of Bradina; it was not tunnel Number 9, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is that first tunnel where we were loaded onto trucks, but this whole night until we arrived at Celebici, until we arrived at tunnel number 9, that was the hardest night.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand what you have been saying, and I am sorry that happened, and thank you very much. You also told the judges that there were no real toilet facilities at Celebici, but you did forget to tell them that there was a bucket provided in Hangar Number 6 at night for you all to use and then it was emptied during the day, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about any buckets. While I was there, there was no bucket. I don't know what happened after I left, but while I was there, there was no bucket.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, all the prisoners that you described from Upper Bradina, you said they received injuries before they were brought to join you in Hangar Number 6, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On that same route from Bradina to Celebici and in Celebici itself, while we were in Number 9, we heard the trouble that they went through until they were placed in Number 6, but I was in no condition to see them, but from the voices and moans that we heard, this was the only thing that we could hear.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you did state before, and I just want to make sure that I understand it, you state that you did not know or recognise any of the guards at Celebici, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will always say that, because I did not know them.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated, I believe, that they just seemed to carry out their instructions and their tasks, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. They could have, but I said a little earlier that right at the beginning it seemed to me that everybody was doing whatever they wanted to. I don't know if somebody was trying to prevent somebody else from doing something. People were doing pretty much what they wanted to do, and according to their purposes, including civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: So there were civilians present that evening; is that what you are saying? I am talking about on May 27th. Did you know that? I am sorry. Let me rephrase that question. I am withdrawing that question actually. Thank you. The prosecution introduced Exhibit Number 83, which was your statement that you gave at Celebici on June 2nd, 1992; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but there are some things that I don't agree with in the statement. I don't agree that I went there and that I was captured there, because you can only say that somebody was captured when there was fighting. We were actually just picked up as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I was going to get to that in my next question. For clarification's sake I was going to ask you that -- you summarised -- in summary the inaccuracies that you claim in the statement were that you didn't go on patrol with the rifle, you merely went to your land to work it, I believe; and also that you never said that Mr Ajanovic was present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I asked those people. They said that I should go to the Commander. I thought that it was Ajanovic, but again from the rumours I heard that that person in charge was Zvonko Zovko.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: The statement you made, excluding the fact that you went on patrol with the rifle and excluding the fact about Mr Ajanovic and -- I have forgotten the term you used -- you were captured -- other than that the statement is fairly accurate, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but I was not captured. Again it is well -- the meaning of the term "captured" is well-known. It can only be during fighting. It is a completely different thing if somebody comes to your house and picks you up.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I agree with you. I think we have an understanding here on what was said. Thank you. Just to clarify, your father was not beaten on May 26th, was he? He was beaten after the military police were killed near your village on July 12th, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I did not mention that, but it is true. Among those police officers they visited us in the sports hall, and they kept telling the elderly people there that we would be returned to our homes, but somebody didn't like that. So on 12th or 13th July the place was completely cleansed and razed to the ground. Right now Bradina is completely cleansed and probably from the entire Konjic municipality there may be a few elderly people here or there, but the entire area has been cleansed. There is no-one alive there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: It would be a fair characterisation that the population responded to the murder of these military police, and that is why Bradina was singled out to be burned on July 12th, whereas the other villages were not; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand fully, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. I will try to repeat again. Bradina was burned to the ground, or more specifically your village of Suljina Strana, I believe, and that was after July 12th, when the military police were murdered close to your village; is that not true? None of the other villages, Bjelovcina or Borci or any of those others, they were not burnt to the ground, were they, just the area where the military police were murdered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually are you trying to ask him to give you a reason why Bradina was burnt?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am trying to make it clear, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You want him to say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I was asking him if he knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to give you an answer. There were a few houses left after 26th, after the night on 27th, but when these police officers were killed up there, I would like to ask you: do you know who killed them? Do you have any information about that, who killed them?

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, I do not know who killed them, but was the popular sentiment not that they thought that the Serbians had done it? The Muslims thought the Serbians had done it for some reason? That is my guess.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was well-known who did it, because we would have been in even worse trouble, but there was nobody there of the Serbs. They did it among themselves. Again I say I don't know who did it. I have absolutely no knowledge of that. It was clear to the entire Konjic and the military there that it was an internal strife, that it was an internal conflict. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your opinion on that. I do not know what is right, because I was not there. Thank you. Just a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You told the judges that a guard from Celebici named Zenga was seen at Musala wearing a white belt; is that not what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, and I noticed him pass by. I saw him twice. I don't know if I saw him any more times.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: And the time that you saw him in Musala with the white belt was some time in July, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was July. I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just another question: the white belt means that he belonged to the military police, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what it meant. That's just what I noticed.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: You only knew the name Zenga and that he was a guard from Celebici from your acquaintances in Musala; would that not be safe to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and we heard rumours about him, that he treated people badly down there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: But you have no personal knowledge about anyone named Zenga yourself, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCMURREY
utterances.text: I pass the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mrs Residovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr Kuljanin, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have to answer all of our questions so every time you feel you need a break, please let me know. My name is Edina Residovic. I am the defence counsel for Zejnil Delalic. We both speak the same language, but it has to be interpreted, and there may be great problems, so I would like to ask you that when I ask you a question, if you could wait with your answer, so that the interpreters can translate, and I will also wait for a while after your answer with my next question. I think that we have reached an agreement on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please allow me to ask you a few general questions which you, as a person born in the Konjic area, would be familiar with. You are aware of the events in the springtime of 1992, so I will concentrate on those. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I am not a native of Konjic, in fact, because I spent all of my working life more in Sarajevo and I had more acquaintances in Sarajevo than Konjic. That's the problem, but I did know some people but not many of them.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, actually I am really glad. My father is also a railroad worker, so we have that in common, but the events in Spring 1992 you are familiar with them, so I will ask a few questions about that. Mr Kuljanin, you gave a statement to the prosecutor on 23rd February 1996 in the US?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some time around that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were told at that time that your statement can be used before the International Tribunal in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you confirmed that what is stated in the statement has been accurately written down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There may be some changes, but I always tried to say the truth, and what I felt that was necessary for me to say. I always say if only we weren't in a position to meet here in this manner, because it would have been better and easier for all of us, and we could have had a different fate, but the events took their turn in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You again confirmed today before the court that you gave a statement in Celebici on 2nd June, and you recognised your signature on that statement. You did make some objections to the contents of the statement. After you arrived in The Hague, have you spoken to the representatives of the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they on that occasion present to you or tell you that they have in their possession your statement given in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that was the way in which you were reminded of what you stated in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is the reason why you remembered today that the rifle that you handed over to those persons from Repovci, that you received that rifle from Slobodan Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These were, in fact, provocations at that time already, because they simply came and they surrounded us on our field and we had to hand it over. I didn't resist. I didn't want to get killed there for no reason.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in the statement that you gave to the prosecutor on 23rd February you did not speak the truth when you said that you bought the rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bought the rifle? I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But in that statement you did not state that you got it from Slobodan Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the statement in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, the statement that you gave later to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. When was I interrogated? I just know that I was interrogated and that I gave the statement in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify the matters. You told me that you gave a statement on 23rd February to the Prosecutor in 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about buying the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you said that you only had a pistol; you forgot to mention the rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time I did not have it when these events took place. I did not have the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuljanin gave you the rifle before the events on 26th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not buy this rifle from Slobodan Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please let me clarify: it was an M-48 rifle. It is a type, a model of rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I guess. As far as I know, these are the old rifles used by the army from before.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is an old army rifle; it is not a hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You could not get a permit for such a rifle according to our laws?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe. You could get a permit for a carbine, but at that time I did not seek a permit. I did not know who to seek it from at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement in Celebici you also said that your son, Novica, had an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He received that rifle from Glavan Vojacic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: His Commander was Petro Djordjic and his Platoon Commander Ramko Djuzar; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you want me to tell you correctly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you do not know, just say "no".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know if they were commanders. I don't know. I can't dream of those things.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you, Mr Kuljanin, in your statement to the Prosecutor, you said none of the inhabitants of Bradina was armed or offered any resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not saying there were no arms but there was no resistance, because if there was resistance, they are casualties on both sides. Some side may be stronger than others, but there are victims on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, before the war you were a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a dual citizenship. At that time there was dual citizenship, Republic of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you were a Yugoslav in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you do not know the regulations, we are not going to discuss them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. No need to.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you have never renounced the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Have you ever officially renounced the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Have you ever requested for your citizenship to be taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you mean "taken away"? For me in every republic you were a citizen of Yugoslavia and that's where I thought my country was. There I was a Croatian, Serbian, Croatian, Macedonia, regardless of where I was. My citizenship was Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was mine too, yes, but in the republics we also had republican ones. All right, Mr Kuljanin. I do not want to discuss these rules, these regulations. I only ask of you: have you ever up until May of 1992 and following May 1992 requested to be -- to leave the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who should I ask that of?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you had a citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know to whom.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you did not ask of anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, and I didn't even have the right conditions for it.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Did you know that in April 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina mobilisation was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whose mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the territorial defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally or your son volunteer to become members of the Territorial Defence of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, but I have a question for you. Can I ask it?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is unusual, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if the Chamber will admit -- well, if they do, did anybody from Bosnia-Herzegovina pull out and renounce the Yugoslav citizenship? Did anybody do that?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know what we are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, here --

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Hercegovina proclaimed its independence and became independent on 6th April 1992 according to the international rules. Okay. What I am asking you: you and your son Novica did not answer to the mobilisation of the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who asked that?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about this Presidency, but please, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You should have answered me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I do not know if you are all having problems, but I cannot understand where one stops and the other one begins with the interpretation. Is there some way that we could either slow it down or -- I think one other time when we did this, they had a different voice for each different party, but I cannot understand which one is which as we are going through. I am asking for clarification on that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have the same difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honour. I will slow it down and maybe we should also change the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I would like that too. Absolutely. That is also sort of shooting the breeze.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, we have an expert and we can continue our discussion later, but now I can continue with the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We do not need to. We are not politicians to be discussing this. We have other things here.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, can you please tell me: do you know Strahinja Zivak, also known as Straho?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He is your neighbour from Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it would be our neighbour from Konjic, you know. That's how we would call it. I am not from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time he was involved to a greater extent in arming the Serbian population in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he personally, before the automatic rifle, had given a semi-automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you, Mr Kuljanin, know that Rajko Djordjic was one of the main organisers in Bradina, ringleaders in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What for?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For what I am talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For something?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For arming and putting blocks around Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if he had anything -- was involved in that, but in what sense do you mention the blocks or blockade of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether the armed population of Bradina put up points in Bradina and people could not travel from Konjic to Sarajevo freely because of those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that that was there. I know there were some checkpoints and that the rail blockade started when the tunnels on both sides of Bradina towards Sarajevo and Konjic were blown up, and then we had a real blockade. When those two tunnels were blown up, then there was the blockade. Now who blew them up ...

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not live there. If somebody was to say that since mid-April from Sarajevo to Konjic and from Konjic to Sarajevo due to the blockade created by Serbs in Bradina you could not travel along the M17 road, you would say that these people who claimed that would be speaking -- would not be speaking the truth; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would not?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If somebody else was to say, if it is written in other documents that after 15th April you could not travel freely through Bradina because of the road blocks put up by the armed population there, that you could not travel to Sarajevo or to Konjic, then these people would be lying; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I will say, when there were barricades put up, could you go to Konjic or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I would appreciate if you would answer my question with an answer and not with a counter-question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will the witness please try only to answer questions and not to ask questions. You are only here to assist the Tribunal. You answer questions. You do not ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But can I -- when I am answering something, can I also ask questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No. You do not ask questions. You answer questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is what it should be here. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Mr Kuljanin, Slobodan Kuljanin gave up the rifle, as we already said. He also gave you 45 bullets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and they took them all away together with the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please tell me, you stated today that you went to your field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not just state that but it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Slobodan Kuljanin give you that rifle for you to take it with you when you planted your potatoes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took it with me.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was probably not the intention of Mr Slobodan Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. We already felt that there were all kinds of bad things going on. There was a blockade and people were accosted and people were -- we did not think that it would be the worst, but we wanted to have it for our personal safety defence. It was not to inflict anything on anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr Kuljanin, your neighbour, Rajko, took a semi-automatic rifle with him on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave to the Prosecutor on 26th February you said that Captain Ajanovic, Hamza Ajanovic, told you about the guarantees for free, unobstructed movement and of the need to surrender the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to me. He was talking that to someone else, but that's how it came out. He was talking about some Nedjo Kuljanin, who was a teacher at that time in the village of Repovci, and the conversation was with him.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I would just like to clarify what you already said. At the time when you were arrested you were arrested, as it is stated in your statement, ten to fifteen persons. You did not recognise any of those persons. Was that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew some by sight but I did not know them by names. You mean when it was in the village or before?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, right at the beginning in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, dear lady, there were not ten or fifteen. The whole village was crawling with soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. I will now quote to you very precisely. You saw many soldiers but: "We were arrested by ten to fifteen armed soldiers."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Arrested whom?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You, you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They found me in front of the house with my wife and children and my elderly father, but if it was -- if that was taking prisoner around the village, there were others.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, you said that your late father was not taken with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They did not take Vaso Kuljanin who was aged 60; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did, but they did not put him in the group of five, six -- there were five or six of them. So they did not put him where they were tying people up, but I was put there.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you also said that you saw HVO soldiers beat or kill your neighbour Drago Kuljanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was that the HVO? I don't know who that was but they had black uniforms. That I saw. I saw that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You gave an answer to that several times, but please clarify to me as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms Residovic, I think we will rise and reassemble at 4 o'clock, so you can continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: (Short break).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness is still on oath. Ms Residovic, carry on with your cross-examination. MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honour. Before the break I had just one question that I wanted to ask before thanking him for his very detailed answers. Mr Kuljanin, you stated before this court that the next day, the second day after your arrival to Celebici, you were given some kind of medical assistance, and then you mentioned the name of a doctor. Is this doctor Ahmet Jusufbegovic and the nurses of the Health Care Centre in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Dr Ahmet Jusufbegovic and I saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since there was an error in the name of the person that you mentioned, you now state that this was Dr Ahmet Jusufbegovic, the manager of the Health Care Centre in Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that I saw Hamo. Is that Ahmet?

utterances.speaker: MS RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He is called Ahmet. Thank you very much. I apologise if some questions were made in such a way that you could not answer precisely. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the last of the cross-examinations? Any re-examination for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no more questions for re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. Are you not exhibiting the document which you were showing the witness, the statement which he made before to the investigator? MS RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now you are discharged. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to thank your Honours. I am noticing that there are people from around the world here, so I would like to thank you and wish you all the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your contribution and assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you again, and again I repeat I wish that we were not here dealing with this matter, but it has to be that way:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. Our next witness is witness F, and I understand that there will have to be some sort of break or recess while the appropriate protective measures are taken in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will it mean more than putting down the screen and making some adjustments?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand from our protection expert Ms van Dusschoten, it is putting up the screen and then lowering all the blinds so the witness can then come to the witness stand and then opening them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That can be done while we are sitting. It will not take too long a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I assume that we will be advised by the video section if there is some additional time needed for the video distortion of the witness's face. I believe they are indicating to me that that is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us carry on with the process of getting it done: I hope there is no reflection inside which might be seen outside. Put down the curtains: Which of the witnesses do you say you are calling? F?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: F is not being shielded from the accused persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Not from the accused persons. I believe this is merely to shield him from the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That screen is obscuring the view of the accused. Now you can see the witness and he can see the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was going to raise that your Honour. One of the important things is to see the demeanour of the witness. I was going to say I could not see him, but I can now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can see from outside whether or not it will be visible from the public gallery. You can go out in the public gallery and see whether or not the witness will be visible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VAN DUSSCHOTEN
utterances.text: I can have a look, but I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It appears that you would be able to see the way they are now; at least from this angle I can see the last two glass panels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We are trying not to obscure the view of the accused persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I am not trying to obscure that view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr Greaves and Mr Mucic need to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I can certainly see Ms McHenry at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What about your client? You can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Might I take instructions from him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: While we are doing this, could I ask Ms McHenry a question about this next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can walk over to her and talk to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is my client cannot, in fact, see the witness from where he is sitting. I would imagine with a little bit of shuffling of chairs the defendants could be asked to move up a bit for just this one witness and endure a bit of discomfort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Pull out that wing of the screen and he might be able to see. There is a possibility of all of them seeing the witness, those behind. THE TECHNICIAN: This way is safe from the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Leave the public alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: A slight suggestion. If we did not raise the last two blinds, that would probably solve the problem. Raise the ones in the middle but not the last ones. THE TECHNICIAN: It's okay like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you can get the witness in. The fear is perhaps there might be a reflection from there showing on the outside screens. That is the fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms McHenry, are you satisfied now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to rely on the experts and if they tell me this is appropriate, I am willing to rely on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are going to proceed, but Ms van Dusschoten is going to go out in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Satisfy yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I just have verification that the video distortion is in place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness. WITNESS F (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Sir, am I correct that you have requested that your name and identity not be released to the public or to the media?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (in interpretation): Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: You will thus be known as Mr F; is that all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Am I correct that you are now 43 years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: In May of 1992 where were you living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bradina, in the hamlet of Krc.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately how big is the hamlet of Krc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very small, eight houses.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who lived in your house with you, sir, not their names but just their relationship, if any, with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife and my child, who was two years old.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: At that time in May of 1992 what was the ethnic background of most of the inhabitants of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: In May of 1992 was there any military action in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not understand. In May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. Was there any fighting or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. When was this that there was some military action in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May 25th 1992 I was at home around 12 o'clock. The shooting started from outside and Bradina is in a valley surrounded by hills. From the hills the shooting commenced. It intensified and after the shooting, the shelling started; the shells started falling around the houses. At that time I came out of the house with my child and went to the basement, which was covered with concrete. That went on until late in the evening. That night I returned to the house, brought some bedding and blankets, returned to the basement with my wife and child and spent the night there. The next day at the break of dawn, that was 26th May 1992, there was mortar and gunfire all over the place. I was in the cellar with my wife and my child, and I was joined by my father, mother and sister. We spent the entire day there in the basement until the evening. In the evening we gathered, people from the village. There was not many of us, and we started to move to go to the village of Barakusa. When we arrived there it was already dark. We arrived in Barakusa where other inhabitants of Upper Bradina and Barakusa had already gathered. There we discussed where to go, what to do and we all spent the night in different houses but also in the basements. Myself, my wife and my child spent the night --

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back for one moment. At the time that the shelling or the shooting started were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How were you armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: How long had you had that rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had it since December of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where did you obtain your rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I bought that rifle because I worked in the restaurant business, and I bought it in front of the restaurant where I worked, and a civilian came and asked how much, since at that time through the media I knew that people were already arming themselves, and because of the fear that I had I bought that weapon and I brought it home. I heard from my mother, who in 1941 remained without her father -- she never met him -- she told me about the events of that time. So because of that fear I bought the rifle. I had two clips with rounds. I never used this gun, because when the shooting started and the shelling from all sides, I was paying more attention to my child than to anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, sir, during the attack did you take part in any armed defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the attack I did not take part in the defence, because that defence did not even exist as far as I know, because on May 25th we were attacked and on 26th already the Lower Bradina was on fire, and I heard later that people had been killed there. On 27th, when I moved to Barakusa, we were surrounded by all sides and they told us to lay down the arms, and I did that as well as the ammunition, the quantities that I had. They registered what I handed over, what it was, and looked whether the rifle was shot from. It was also interesting that there was a foreigner, who was wearing a black uniform, and he was checking the weapons. Of the people there I recognised Redzo Balic, but the rest I did not know when they came over to us.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Had that weapon been fired? Were they able to verify whether or not the weapon had been fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This foreign national checked it and saw that the weapon had not been fired.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What happened next, sir, briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that they lined us up. There were women and children and elderly, and we, the villagers from the three villages, the Lower Bradina, Donje Selo and Barakusa, we started towards Bradina. We came 1 km off Bradina to Mica Kuljanin's cafe. They separated us from the elderly people and from the women. The women were put in front of Dragan Subotic's house and they put us in front of Mica's cafe. They were taking out all things from the cafe, whereas the elderly were across the street, on the other side from us. Then they told us to turn over all our belongings that we had on us. That's when they took all the personal jewellery, the money and watches that we had. They took that, and then they started beating us. I was the second. In front of me was Zdravko Gligorevic, who was an attorney in Sarajevo. His parents lived there, so he came to visit. He had a beard and they beat him until he fell unconscious, and then they turned to me and they beat me. It was a sort of a cable and they beat me over the head, and I fell unconscious. This was all observed by my wife, my parents and my child. After I fell unconscious -- I don't know how long that lasted -- they took us further towards Bradina, more precisely, to the tunnel where the railroad tracks were, and there was a retaining wall which was five or six metres tall. Then they lined us up against a wall. We put our hands up, took off our shoes, and they searched us again, and they said that they -- they wrote down everything we had.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go please a little more slowly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the meantime while we were being searched a truck with a canopy arrived and behind this vehicle there were soldiers in camouflage uniforms standing on both sides.
