We had to pass them in order to climb into the vehicle. At that time I was maybe the sixth or the seventh, but as each person passed, they beat them with some sticks, with rifle butts, and pieces of wood, I don't know how to explain them, with many different objects that were at hand. We climbed in the vehicle and when we all climbed in, they pulled down the canvas of the canopy and then we were in the van for about one hour and then we started going towards Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where were you brought, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to Celebici. That was the camp where I spent six months. When we arrived to Celebici, they pulled up the canopy, and -- I apologise. What I skipped, when we climbed onto the vehicle, we were stripped. We only kept tee-shirts or shirts. Then we climbed down from the vehicle and they lined us up against a wall which was something like 3 metres tall, and we had to put our hands up. When we all climbed onto the vehicle, they started beating us.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt for one second. What was the date then when you were actually brought to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 27th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately what time of day was it when you were brought to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was between 12 and 1 o'clock, but since nobody had a watch -- all that had been taken away from us -- I think it could have been between 12 and 1.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many persons were brought to Celebici at the same time as you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came along the way, they also picked up people from Kuljani, and that was across from Mica's cafe, and houses were already on fire and the whole village was burning. Then further down at the Jaila restaurant the others who lived around that area were also picked up. So there was about 70-80 people from Bradina altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Please continue with what happened when you first arrived at Celebici. What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time terrible beatings started with different objects. We were leaning against a wall in shirts and undershirts. They beat us with crowbars, with sticks, with rifle butts, kicked us and there were a lot of them, and they took turns. I heard my father's wailing. He was born in 1926. He was five or six people to the right of me, and then he said "Zovko, please don't." "Who is Zovko?", and cursed him. He said: "I'll gag you with the sock." That hurt me more than everything I had suffered until that moment. Then Milan Gligorevic, the third person away from me, lay down on the asphalt, and started beating him mercilessly. He was telling me to lie down on the asphalt and kiss it and start pulling my own hair. I did it. It was a person that I don't know who it was. He said: "That's not how you do it." Then he took me by the hair and hit my head into the asphalt and that pain started. They beat me with all kinds of objects and I injured my left arm below -- above the hand, and I had a partial fracture. Then I started groaning. When it was over, they turned me back and started beating me with the rifle butts again and told me to raise my arms again. I couldn't raise it because it hurt so much I could not hold it. They beat me again with rifle butts. Then I dropped to my knees, and I asked them to give me some water, because I was thirsty. There was something like a stream. It was not a stream really. There was some water down there. Then he told me: "Here, you cattle, go and drink." Then I started drinking and he said: "Enough. That's enough!" Then I returned to the wall and I stood there without being able to lift my arm. To the left of me stood Miroslav Vujcic and next to him his brother, Radoslav. At that time they told Mirosalv Vujcic to step out and lie down on the asphalt. He knelt and then they hit him several times. When he saw what I had gone through and what he was about to get, he started running, and, maybe it was about 20 metres of me, somebody said: "Shoot", and then there was a burst of fire. It was heard and Miroslav was killed there. His brother Radoslav, who was standing next to me, said: "My God! They killed my brother, Miro." The person who did that was a certain Makaron. We stood there. They kept beating us. They ordered if somebody else attempted to escape that they should be shot, but you could not run away anywhere because everything was fenced off. We stood there until the evening. I do not recall how long. Then we were brought to the Hangar Number 6, and it was dark by that time, and they turned on the lights. The hangar was empty, a concrete floor. We sat down there and we spent the night; that night we spent there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you were being beaten on the 27th in Celebici, could you tell whether or not the people were soldiers or civilians or from certain military groups? Can you tell us what you could observe concerning that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were people in camouflage uniforms and in black uniforms as far as I could see, but since I was facing the wall I don't know how many of them there were, and many of them took turns doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you see whether or not the people in camouflage uniforms, what kind of insignia they had, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see anything at that time, because I was facing the wall.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did I understand you correctly that the brother of Miro Vujcic, Radoslav Vujcic, that he was standing next to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the killing of Miroslav he was standing next to me. There was Miroslav Vujcic, Radoslav Vujcic, his brother, and then when they took out Miroslav, Radoslav remained next to me, standing to my left.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: To your knowledge were any other detainees seriously injured or killed during that occasion on the 27th, when you arrived in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that day. We were transferred to Number 6. I lay there and then after a while -- I don't know how many days -- the men who had been brought in on 26th May, who were in Number 9, were transferred to Number 6. They were all bandaged up, black and blue. Their heads were injured and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you -- you were brought to hangar 6. Can you briefly describe what happened the next day, after you were in hangar 6? I am sorry. Can you describe what happened to you that night, if anything, in Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was brought in that night in Hangar Number 6 some persons unknown to me came in. I don't know -- I didn't know them. They looked at us. They talked to each other. They were saying things I don't remember now, because I was in a very serious condition that night until the next morning, and then the next morning we were taken out to urinate to the left of the hangar. There was a concrete pavement there. At the exit to the hangar a soldier in an army uniform sat on a wooden crate. He had crutches next to him. It was at the entrance to the hangar on the left-hand side. Since I held my left arm in my right hand and my shirt was pulled out of my trousers, he told me: "Why do you look like that?" I told him that I could not do anything about it, because my arm hurt. So I listened to his orders and I went in and sat on my place. Radoslav Vujicic sat next to me and I told him about it. He told me that he used to work with that man and that his name was Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you say that you obeyed his orders, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry. Did you just state that the person with crutches, you listened to his orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What orders were those? Can you just explain that? Did he tell you to do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My shirt was outside of my trousers and my undershirt, and he told me to put it in. He told me that I should pull myself together, and look tidy. I could not do that because my left arm was hurting, and I was holding it with my right hand. So I pulled up my trousers. I managed to do that with just one hand, and I went in and sat down on my place.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Were there other prisoners in Hangar Number 6 before you and the group you were with were brought to hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hangar?

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of the 80 people, all of the people, us people were Bradina, all 80 of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Your question probably was a different one. Was the hangar empty at that time when he went?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if you know, before the group of 80 people were brought to hangar 6, were there already other prisoners being kept in Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We were the first ones to arrive in Hangar Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: After your group was brought into Celebici, in the next -- in the subsequent days were other detainees brought to Celebici, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After a certain time -- I don't recall exactly how many days it was -- a group of people was brought in. They were brought into Celebici on 26th May, and they were located in Number 9, and then they were transferred from Number 9 to our place. There were about 70 of them, something like that, 70, maybe 80. I don't know how many of them.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were there also other detainees in the next week after you were brought to Celebici, where detainees were brought in from outside the camp, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember how many days later. Some people were brought in from Celebici, Bjelovcina; later from Brdjani, Konjic and other places.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you observe about what happened to them when they were brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those second group that came in from Number 9, they had been beaten very severely, and you can see that on their faces, because they had been beaten all over their heads. Some had bandages on their head. Some were black and blue. Some had bruises on the eye or under it. You could see the marks, the wounds on their heads. These were the people who had been brought it on the 26th before us and then they were placed in Number 9 and transferred later to our place.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember any specific detainees whose injuries you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember Vukasin Mrkajic, who was all black and blue. I could hardly recognise him. I remember Mirko Kuljanin who had a bandage on his head. There were quite a few of them but I can't remember now. It's been five years now so I can't remember their names, but there were quite a few of them with serious injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was there a time when -- soon after you were brought to Celebici -- when there was a group of persons brought in who had come from the Igman area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could hear later, people from the Igman area were brought into Number 9 and those people from Number 9 were transferred to Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember any detainees from that group, and if you observed anything about their condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The detainees were in a serious condition when they were transferred from Number 9 to Number 6. One couldn't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I just remember one group arrived from Igman. Pero Mrkajic, Radoslav Kuljanin and others were among them. They were brought in at night. This was horrible, the moans, the cries, the screams. Then they were put in Number 6. There was no light. It was dark. We didn't know who they were, but then when the day broke, we saw who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was one of those people Pero Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: What was his condition at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you saw him the next morning in Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in a really bad condition. When he was thrown in he fell right in front of my legs. He lay down there and that's where he remained. In the morning we moved a bit and he sat next to me, third or fourth from me. He could hardly breathe and he couldn't speak. Later on they brought in a wooden crate and he lay on it for a while. He couldn't go out. Stevo Gligorevic helped him out and Bosko Samoukovic helped him later. As for the food we received which was really minimal, a slice of bread, he couldn't eat that either. He was there for a while and then he was transferred to number 22, and later I heard that he died in number 22.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you approximate for me when it was that Pero Mrkajic was brought into Hangar Number 6? About how long had you been in Celebici when he were brought into the hangar approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't remember exactly, but I think it was at the beginning of June. I can't recall the exact date. The beginning of June, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, if you know, approximately how many people were kept in Hangar Number 6 during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a while there were 248 of us there, people in Number 6. Then the people from Brdjani, Bjelovcina, Cerici, Donje Selo, Konjic and other villages such as Blace were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe for the court what the conditions were like when you were kept in Hangar Number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were really bad. The floor was concrete. We lay down on the concrete. The food was virtually non-existent. We got -- our meals consisted of one slice of bread and these meals were not regular. Each loaf of bread was cut into 12 or 15 slices. Later on we got some soup, and we were only allowed two spoonfuls. I remember on one occasion Drago Djordjic took one more spoonful and then he was beaten for that, and five or six spoons -- five or six, I can't recall exactly, were for the use of all of us and we ate from the same bowl. This was not washed at all. It was all placed on a crate. At first it was located to the right of the entrance on a wooden crate, and some people didn't dare to go out, because they were afraid they would be beaten, and later on the food was distributed inside the hangar close to the door, again to the right. The conditions were really very bad. We went to the toilet in the morning and in the evening at first. We lay down on the concrete floor. The conditions were really extremely bad.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you interrogated while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the beginning of June. I can't remember the exact date. I think it was either 2nd, 3rd or the 4th June. We were taken somewhere towards the entrance, to the gate. I was questioned outside of a building. I don't remember precisely, because I was very afraid. We went up there and we were questioned.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you remember who questioned you, what kinds of questions were asked? Can you please describe that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember very precisely. I remember that they asked me if I had any weapons. "Yes." "Were you a member of the SDS?" "Yes." "Did you fire your weapon?" "No." "Are you sure?" "I'm sure." "How much ammunition did you have?" I said how much ammunition I had. That was 60 rounds, and I signed something there and that was it. They also asked me where I was at the time and I explained everything, just as I said to you, that I was at home with my child and my wife in the basement and that I went to Barakusa. I explained everything to them on the occasion of my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you able to read this statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, besides what you have already told us about, did you observe any mistreatment while you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would like you to go, please, very slowly, and if you can give an approximate time, if you remember, and just describe one incident at a time. Can you please tell us the first incident that you remember besides what you have already told us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first incident that happened in the camp was again some time in June. I don't know the exact date. When we were supposed to go to urinate, I was among the first to get out. I went to the hole that was dug up to the right of the hangar. Then I started to defaecate and three people came. They wore camouflage uniforms and had automatic weapons with them. They passed me by. I got up, and they told me to squat down and to defecate on the five-point star, and then I saw below me there was a police hat with the star, and I remained there. They went on to the hangar. I don't know who it was who they called out, but I heard the noise in front of the hangar, and I heard blunt blows. All of a sudden there was a burst of fire. I jumped up, pulled up my trousers and ran into the hangar. In the meantime I saw Miso Kuljanin, nicknamed Coba. The three of them were standing above him and he tried to get up two or three times, and then he was dead. I ran into the hangar without even buttoning up my trousers. I sat down, and the whole thing quietened down. Then later on the same day some people came in. I don't remember who they were. They asked: "Who witnessed the murder of Miso?" Since it was the turn of five or six people to go out, Janko Glogovac, Spasoje Miljevic and Zjelko Cecez saw that, and they asked Janko Glogovac: "Did you see it?", and he said: "No". They said, going to Cecez: "Did you see this?" He said: "Yes". They took him out for a while and he went back in. I didn't dare to say that I also saw that. So I escaped that fate, and they again said: "Did anyone else see?" I did not say that I had seen, and that same night Zjelko Cecez was taken out at night. I don't know who took him out, because it was at night. He went out and we could hear -- you could hear his moans for a while, and then after a while he was thrown into the hangar. Then his moans were heard in the hangar. He was asking for water. I don't know if anyone gave him some water, and in the morning we saw Zjelko Cecez dead. He was on the floor with one arm stretched out and one arm next to his body. He was dead there, that morning.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you said you did not see who took him out, because it was dark, was the hangar lighted at night -- hangar lit at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The only time that the hangar was lit was the first night when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you ever witness any other acts of mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember a man by the name of Jovanovic. He was an elderly man. He sat next to the tin sheet, next to the entrance. One night he was called out by Esad Landzo, nicknamed Zenga. He got out and also he had gotten out before that. He had been called out before and on that night when he was called out, he was most likely beaten, because we could hear in the hangar his moans --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to this line of questioning. First of all he said the hangar was dark and now he says he identifies someone but he also said he heard something outside but he does not know what went on outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can cross-examine him when your turn comes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it was dark. There was no light, but when I say that Landzo took him out, he has a very peculiar voice, and I was able to recognise him. I should have told you -- I am sorry -- that I recognised his voice. Everybody in the hangar knew his voice. When he spoke, everybody knew. We heard the moans because the sheet metal, the tin, was the only thing that stood between us. He was crying for his mother. That's what we heard. Then he was brought back in and he was dead in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you estimate approximately when this was that Mr Jovanovic was taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In June. It was in June.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you describe any other incidents that you have information -- that you have knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Bosko Samoukovic, who sat on the same side at the entrance on the opposite side of the entrance next to the tin, he was taken out by Landzo, and Landzo asked him: "What's your name?" "My name is Bosko Samoukovic". He had on a railway worker's shirt. First he beat him on the sides and then he told him: "Take off the shirt." He took a plank, which is maybe 5 or 6 cms wide, and beat him on the kidneys until he knocked him down, and when he knocked him down, he started beating him with a rifle butt.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where was this happening, sir? Where was the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened in the hanger in front of all of us. We were all able to see that. He beat him with the rifle butt until he fainted. He was then taken out and then Brane Gligorevic got out. He was a male nurse. He worked as a nurse in the Konjic hospital. Then when he got back he said he was sitting as the second to my left, and he said that his tongue had fallen into his throat and that he had managed to pull it out. He was then transferred to number 22. The next day -- all this was happening in front of us, and two of his sons, Milan Samoukovic and Nedeljko Samoukovic, and his brother, Spasoje. Then the next morning Hazim Delic came, and, as usual, it was well-known who he would be beating. Nedeljko Samoukovic, his son, was among that group. He told him to get up and everybody knew what he was supposed to do, to put up his arms and turn his back, but Nedjo asked him in the meantime: "Excuse me, sir, Commander, can I ask you, how is my father?" He said: "Which one?" "The one who was taken in last night, Bosko Samoukovic". He looked him in the eye and said: "He's dead. Sit down." Then Nedjo Samoukovic was not beaten that day, although he was beaten regularly every day and abused with Vukasin Mrkajic, Dusko Bendjo.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Could you please tell us in what way they were mistreated? What were you able to observe about how Nedeljko Samoukovic and these other people were treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every morning when he got into the Number 6, Hazim Delic would come to Samoukovic, I mean Nedeljko Samoukovic. He would make two steps, put his hands behind his head and then he would kick him. Sometimes he would kick him on both sides; sometimes several times, or also sometimes he carried a bat, a wooden bat. I heard later that it was called a baseball bat, he used it to beat people with. He was the person whom he beat most severely together with Vukasin Mrkajic, Dusko Bendjo, and then Vukalo, whose first name I forgot. They were beaten almost every day. Also Radoslav Kuljanin, and as for Landzo, he had the same people plus Zoran Djordjic, and also some other people that he would pick out, but these were the regulars.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say that Landzo had some of these same people, what do you mean he had some of these same people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean to say that when Delic was not around he was doing the same thing with these people. He was making them get up and beating them, and in addition to them, those other people that I named, Zoran Cecez, as I said, Drago Djordjic, and many, many others whose names I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you say he was doing the same things to this group of people, who is the "he" you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean Esad Landzo, nicknamed Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: You also, sir, mentioned Radoslav Kuljanin. Can you tell us what, if anything, you observed happened to Radoslav Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I am correct you just indicated that you saw Radoslav Kuljanin mistreated. Did you observe Radoslav Kuljanin ever being mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radoslav Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Excuse my pronunciation. Yes, sir. Can you please tell us what, if anything, you observed with respect to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Radoslav Kuljanin was brought in from Igman, he was beaten at the entrance to the hangar, and he sat right to the left of the entrance, and he couldn't for maybe five or six days eat. He couldn't open his eyes, and he just drink some water, and he could hardly move. He was really very badly beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is that the only time that you yourself saw Mr Kuljanin, Radoslav, mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that Radoslav Kuljanin was also beaten in front of all of us. That was done by Hazim Delic. He beat him several times and every morning he knew and he would say: "Oh, my God! Here it comes!" Then he started begging: "Please don't beat me", but he was beaten every morning, like all the other people that I mentioned just now.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was there a detainee named Scepo Gotovac in the camp to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately how old was Mr Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was born in 1921 or 1922.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where did he sit approximately in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He sat right next to the entrance to the right. He was the first one, because he was the first one who got in that day. I remember very well when Scepo Gotovac arrived, he sat behind the door to the right. Then after a while -- I don't know how long a period of time -- Hazim Delic walked in. He had a paper in his hand, and he read out very loudly so that everybody could hear "Gotovac, Scepo". He said: "I am." He said: "Get up." He got up and then he said: "In 1942, I think, you killed on this very spot two Muslims and you will stay here", and he said: "This is not true. I don't know anything about that." He hit him several times about the head and once in the stomach, and he fell down. Then he took him away -- he took him by the shoulder, pushed him out, and then one could hear his cries. He was thrown in and for a time actually until the evening it lasted, and then he was called out again. I don't know who it was who called him. He said: "I can't get up." "Carry him out." Somebody carried him out. Then after more moans from him, he was brought back in. Then in the morning they said that Scepo was dead. So he came in, he was beaten and he died on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, while you were at the camp did you have occasion to hear about an alleged incident in Repovci? Let me spell this for the translators, please. R-E-P-O-V-C-I, Repovci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately when was this that you heard about this alleged incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that incident I think on the same day. Zmijomesa came to the Celebici camp and said that some police officers were killed near Repovci and that night there will be trouble. That night, that evening, I think in the afternoon -- I don't know what the exact time was -- Hazim Delic came and said: "What are you guys doing up there? They are killing our police officers", and he cursed our mother. Then he started beating people one by one, and he ordered Zenga: "This is what the people from Bradina are to get for breakfast, lunch and dinner", and from that day on in the evening we did not receive any dinner. We were forbidden water, food. All of us from Bradina had to get up, and Zenga continued with his game. From that day on every single day we were beaten one by one. Zenga went from one to another and beat us.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Approximately how long did this treatment last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It lasted for a time. I don't know how long. I can't remember, but it was quite a long time. I think maybe until the time when Bosko Samoukovic was killed, that we were beaten regularly every day, we people from Bradina. We had to get up every morning, the people from Bradina, and every day it went on. We were even forbidden water and food and other things. It was really so hot and very hard without the water.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you yourself beaten during these occasions, or just other people from Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten on that day, when this happened, when Hazim Delic came, and then again on one occasion by Landzo, nicknamed Zenga. He kicked me twice, and that was all, but he beat the others regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was there a detainee named Zjelko Klimenta in the camp, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what, if anything, you observed happened to him and the approximate time-frame, if you know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in early August. Zjelko Klimenta sat in the corner, five people away from me, in the very corner of the hangar, and then one morning, it was early, about 5.00 am, Zoran Tomovic came for him and told him to go out and have coffee with him. He said: "I don't want to." So he went back and then later on somebody called him from the outside. I don't know who it was. He got up. He was in a grumpy mood. He went out. After a time we heard a shot. Kujundzic and Zoran Tomovic walked in. Kujundzic held his head in his hands and he said: "Keljo was killed." That's what he was called, Keljo, and he sat down in his place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is a convenient point to stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning we will continue with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I just ask the witness, just to be clear, the witness to stay where he is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness stay where he is. Do not move until we all get out. The Trial Chamber will rise and reassemble tomorrow morning at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --ooOoo--
